title: Kori rotti: crisp wafers, coastal curry
body: Kori rotti is one of the best-known dishes of the Tulu-speaking coast. It pairs a rich chicken curry, kori gassi, with rotti: thin, dry rice wafers made in a separate batch and toasted until they snap.

The trick is timing. The curry is ladled over the wafers just before eating, so they soften at the edges and stay crisp in the middle. The gravy is built on coconut and dried red chillies, often with tamarind for a slight sourness.
Many families serve it at weddings and festive lunches, and the dish shows how much of the coastal kitchen depends on coconut, rice and chilli, the three things the region grows best.

title: Yakshagana: a stage that runs until sunrise
body: Yakshagana is the traditional theatre of coastal Karnataka. It combines dance, music, spoken dialogue and elaborate costume, and a performance often begins after dark and runs until dawn.

The story is usually taken from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata or the Puranas. A singer, the Bhagavata, narrates while musicians play the chende and maddale drums, cymbals and a harmonium. The actors improvise their spoken parts within the outline of the tale.

The tall headgear, painted faces and bright skirts of the characters are made by hand. Two main styles are recognised, Tenkuthittu in the south and Badagutittu in the north. Troupes travel across Dakshina Kannada and Udupi in the cooler months, and a village show can draw a crowd from several neighbouring villages.

title: St Mary's Islands: the rock that looks like stacked pencils
body: Off the coast at Malpe, near Udupi, four small islands rise from the Arabian Sea. The most visited is Coconut Island, where visitors arrive by ferry from the harbour.

The islands are known for their columns of basalt, packed side by side and often six-sided. Geologists link them to volcanic activity tens of millions of years ago, and the site is listed among India's national geological monuments.

There is a tradition that the explorer Vasco da Gama landed here in 1498 and set up a cross, and the name of the islands is said to come from that visit. The ferries run in the fair-weather season and are usually stopped during the monsoon, when the sea is rough.

title: Kambala: racing through the paddy slush
body: Kambala is the buffalo race of coastal Karnataka. Pairs of buffaloes are driven through a flooded, muddy paddy track by a farmer who runs behind, holding a rope and a plough or a wooden board.

The season usually runs from about November to March, after the harvest. Winners are judged on speed and on how high the mud is thrown, and the events are held across Dakshina Kannada and Udupi, drawing large crowds.

Kambala began as a farmers' celebration of the harvest, and today it is a major sporting tradition with its own rules and a governing body, though it has also drawn debate about the treatment of the animals.

title: Malpe harbour: where the catch comes in
body: Malpe is one of the busiest fishing harbours on Karnataka's coast. Mechanised trawlers and purse-seine boats leave in the evening and return the next morning, and the harbour is crowded with auction bids, ice and shouting.

Oil sardine, called boothai locally, and Indian mackerel, called bangude, are two of the most important species in the west coast catch. The sea's abundance varies from year to year with the monsoon and water temperature.

During the monsoon, from the start of June to the end of July, a fishing ban on mechanised boats applies along the west coast so that fish can breed. Boats are pulled up, nets are mended, and the harbour is quiet until August.

title: Kudremukh: the horse-face mountain
body: Kudremukh, in the Western Ghats of Chikkamagaluru district, gets its name from the Kannada for horse face, because one of its peaks resembles a horse's head in profile.

The hills are covered in shola forest and grassland, and much of the area is a national park. The lion-tailed macaque, one of the rarest monkeys in the world, lives in the forests of the Western Ghats, which are also a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Several rivers begin in these hills. The Netravati, which passes Bantwal and meets the sea at Mangaluru, is among them. When the rain falls on Kudremukh, the water it sends down is the same that later fills the wells and rivers of the coast.

title: Udupi Krishna Matha: the window of nine holes
body: The Sri Krishna Matha in Udupi is the centre of the Dvaita tradition founded by Madhvacharya, who is said to have installed the idol of Krishna here in the 13th century.

Worshippers do not enter the sanctum. They see the idol through a small window called the Navagraha Kindi, a silver-plated window with nine holes. A nearby window, the Kanakana Kindi, is linked to the poet-saint Kanakadasa.

The temple is managed by eight monasteries, the Ashta Mathas, whose heads take turns to run it in a cycle called the Paryaya, which changes every two years. The kitchen serves thousands of meals, and the town's vegetarian cooking traditions grew around it.
